title: Growing English Ivy Indoors

paragraphs.heading: Ornamental Features
paragraphs.text: Ornamental ivies have an amazing range of different foliage types. Many ivies have leaves edged, splashed or centered with silver, gray-green, white, cream, yellow, chartreuse or gold.

paragraphs.heading: Problems
paragraphs.text: In the home, plant diseases are very rarely a problem. Too much or too little water plus insects and mites are the main problems. Root rot usually results from a soil mix that does not drain quickly or overly frequent watering.

paragraphs.heading: Problems
paragraphs.text: Mealybugs, mites, aphids, whiteflies and scales are the most common insect pests of ivies grown as houseplants. For more information on Common Houseplant & Insect Pest, see HGIC 2252 Common Houseplant Insects & Related Pests . If the area infested is limited you can prune out those parts of the plant. Periodic washing can help prevent many pest problems. Wash plants by dunking the foliage upside down in a gallon of water to which insecticidal soap has been added. Hold the soil in the pot with a cover of foil or plastic.

paragraphs.heading: Problems
paragraphs.text: Maintaining cooler temperatures and high humidity will help prevent some of the most common insect pests, but the plant will grow more slowly.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Most cultivars of ivy grow best in bright light, but not direct sun. They tolerate low to medium light, but growth is reduced and variegated forms may turn all green. To maintain the bright color of a variegated ivy, give it plenty of light. Ivies can be grown with artificial light, or near a north, east or west window.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Water ivies thoroughly, then let the soil dry to the touch to a depth of ½ inch before watering again. Although ivies prefer moderate humidity, they will tolerate normal low home levels. Raise the humidity by setting the plants on a tray of wet pebbles or perlite. Do not allow ivies to stand in water. Ivies benefit from good air circulation, and they should not be crowded.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Ivies do well at cool to moderate room temperatures of 50 to 70 °F during the day and about 5 to 10 °F lower at night.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Fertilize ivies monthly while they are actively growing with a foliage houseplant fertilizer, according to the label directions. Do not use fertilizer when plants stop growing either in the heat of summer, or when temperatures are cool.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Propagation is by rooting stem or tip cuttings. Most types of ivy will root easily in water. Repot ivies when the plants become top-heavy or root bound or dry out too rapidly. The new pot should be no more than 1 inch larger in diameter than the pot it was originally grown in. Using too large a pot can cause the soil to stay wet too long and lead to root rot.

paragraphs.heading: Culture
paragraphs.text: Ivy topiaries are made by planting a small-leafed ivy cultivar at the base of a sphagnum moss- stuffed wire frame. The plants are kept trained and pinned to the frame. They need to be pruned frequently to keep the shape clear. Sometimes two types of ivy will be grown on a frame to show details, such as eyes, on an animal topiary. Be especially careful to keep the upper portions of a topiary moist.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: The American Ivy Society describes ivy cultivars by leaf shape and by plant type if unusual. Leaf shapes are ivy with typical flat leaves that have 5 lobes; heart-shaped which may also be triangular, with 3 lobes; fan shaped are triangular or have lobes pointing forward; bird's foot with narrow lobes or willow-like leaves; and curly leaves are ruffled, rippled or wavy.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: Plant types include miniatures, small plants with leaves under 1inch long; oddities, which have unusual traits such as distorted or curly stems or leaves, or bushy upright growth; and variegateds, which have leaves of more than one color, or a color other than green.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Buttercup' has pale green leaves in shade, bright yellow in sun.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Caecilia' has variegated, curly leaves that are rounded and frilled. They are light green with gray blotches and white edges.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Curly Locks' has large, rounded curly leaves with rippled lobes.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Fluffy Ruffles' has small, curly leaves with frilled margins.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: ‘Gold Child’ English ivy ( Hedera helix ‘Gold Child’) is one of the more popular variegated ivies. Barbara H. Smith. ©2015 HGIC, Clemson Extension 'Gold Child' has soft mottled green leaves with bright cream yellow margins that are larger and wider than those of other gold-edged cultivars.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Gold Heart' has heart-shaped leaves with a bold splash of creamy yellow in the center.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Ivalace' has very glossy curly leaves that are blackish green in color with wavy, crimped margins.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Manda Crested' Large, very curly leaves on a fast and easy-to-grow vine.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Parsley Crested' has heavily crested, curly round leaves on thick upright stems.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Sagittaefolia Variegata' is a birds foot ivy with white-frosted foliage.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Spectre' is a unique clumping runner with large leaves, dappled cream and gray. The leaves are curled and twisted.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Spetchley' has very tiny-blackish-green, triangular leaves that are maroon when young. The stems are straight, stiff and very dark.

paragraphs.heading: Cultivars
paragraphs.text: 'Telecurl' has showy, large ruffled leaves.
